sources.judgment: I5.4 states the decreasing-psh limit property by reference to the preceding subharmonic case; no nonexistent separate printed full proof is claimed. Its application can be reconstructed directly: on each small ball the radial truncations have a common upper bound, are psh by nonnegative nondecreasing logarithmic slopes, and decrease. Their limit is usc, and monotone convergence of the upper-bound-minus-potential passes every complex-line submean inequality, including the canonical minus-infinity value at the pole. I5.8's whole positive-Hessian representative proof was read. The smooth radial Hessian criterion explicitly allows semipositivity, so density zeros require no strict Hessian assumption.

The complete bounded corrected expansion and Proposition2.1 proof, including positivity by closed local approximations and the epsilon limit, were reread. Its antecedent is Ti>=0, so the new semipositive radial current at a smooth density zero is admitted. On compact finite-level subsets the actual potential is bounded, exact locality identifies the ordinary radial determinant, and exclusion of the pole plus the explicit integrable density gives mass one. Conditional product truncations are actual pullbacks; dimensions leave exactly binomial(m+k,m)h0^m wedge q kappa^k, and multiplying by the strict superlevel removes boundary-level contributions. No Section2.2 unbounded theorem, BMP, global exact Hermitian smoothing or mass invariance for nonclosed backgrounds is imported.

new_elementary_application_judgment: The relative central tail forces q positive near the pole despite allowing zeros elsewhere. Every positive radius therefore has M(r)>0. Its positive kth root stays smooth across any zero of q, with Q'>=0, so the inverse potential and residual are smooth there. At infinity the smooth radial t=1/r density and probability normalization give smooth M,Q with Q(0)=P(0)=1. The zero-annulus example has exactly the baseline central mass near the pole; hence its residual is constant there and globally smooth. All earlier endpoint and flat-error estimates persist. These are proved radial geometric hypotheses, not an assertion of regularity from density smoothness alone.
